evidence: The sequence has N-terminal LDL-receptor class A repeats, EGF-like domains, four YWTD beta-propellers, a transmembrane segment and an NPxY cytoplasmic tail, which looks like LRP4, an agrin/Wnt co-receptor at the neuromuscular junction. I know of no established virus-receptor role for LRP4, unlike relatives such as VLDLR, LRP8 or LDLRAD3, so this is a moderate-confidence call.

The sequence has no recognizable signal peptide, transmembrane anchor, or known receptor domain, so nothing supports a role as a host cell-surface virus receptor. Its composition looks unusual and possibly fragmentary, so this judgment rests on missing evidence rather than a confident identification.

The sequence looks like an LRP4-type LDL receptor-related protein, with eight LDLa repeats, EGF-like modules, four YWTD beta-propellers, a single transmembrane segment and a short cytoplasmic tail. These proteins act mainly in agrin/MuSK and Wnt signalling, and nothing in the sequence indicates direct cholesterol binding.

The sequence has no recognizable cholesterol-binding module, such as a sterol-sensing domain, START domain, OSBP-related ligand-binding domain, NPC2/MD-2 fold or CRAC/CARC-rich transmembrane segments. Its composition looks atypical and possibly artificial, so this is a judgment from absence of features rather than a confident negative.

The sequence looks like LRP4: eight LDLR class A repeats, EGF-like domains, four YWTD beta-propellers, a transmembrane segment and an NPxY cytoplasmic motif. LRP4 plausibly acts as an adaptor that links agrin to MuSK at the neuromuscular junction, but I cannot confirm from memory that this specific GO term is assigned to it.

No recognizable adaptor or scaffold domains or binding motifs (e.g., SH2/SH3, WD40, armadillo, PDZ) can be identified in this long sequence, which has an unusual, possibly low-complexity composition. Nothing in the sequence alone supports protein-macromolecule adaptor activity, so this is a weak, mainly base-rate call.

The sequence has a signal peptide, multiple LDL-receptor class A repeats, EGF-like domains, four YWTD beta-propellers and a single transmembrane segment, which marks it as an LRP4-like cell-surface receptor. Such a protein would not be expected to bind nucleosomes.

The sequence has no recognizable nucleosome-interacting domains (such as bromo-, chromo-, PHD, SANT/SWIRM or SNF2-type ATPase domains), and its unusual, low-complexity composition looks scrambled or non-natural. Nothing supports annotating it with nucleosome binding.

The sequence is a dTDP-glucose 4,6-dehydratase (TGDS-like) of the SDR/NAD-epimerase family. It has no signal peptide or transmembrane segment, so it is most likely a soluble cytosolic enzyme. I recall no Golgi localization for this protein, though I can't fully rule out an imaging-based Golgi annotation.

The sequence has several N-glycosylation motifs and looks like a secretory-pathway glycosyltransferase (possibly an O-fucosyltransferase or CAP10-like enzyme), and many such enzymes are Golgi-resident. However, related enzymes (e.g., POFUT/POGLUT) sit in the ER, and no Golgi-specific targeting signal can be identified from this fragment alone.

The sequence looks like human dTDP-D-glucose 4,6-dehydratase (TGDS), an NAD-dependent epimerase/dehydratase family enzyme that dehydrates nucleotide sugars. As far as I recall, it is not established as part of glycosaminoglycan biosynthesis, though its exact physiological role is unclear.

The sequence has no recognizable glycosyltransferase or sulfotransferase motifs typical of glycosaminoglycan synthases, such as the clear DXD motifs of the EXT, chondroitin or hyaluronan synthase families. Its several N-glycosylation sites suggest only a secreted or luminal protein of unclear function, so a GAG biosynthetic role is not supported, though the protein could not be identified with confidence.

This looks like a TGDS/RmlB-type extended SDR, with the TGxxGxxG NAD-binding motif, the YxxxK catalytic motif (YASSK) and the dehydratase-specific DEVYG motif. These features support dTDP-glucose 4,6-dehydratase activity, though the call rests on motif and family similarity rather than direct evidence for this protein.

The sequence lacks the N-terminal Rossmann-fold GxxGxxG NAD-binding motif and the conserved catalytic YxxxK/TGG features of SDR-family RmlB enzymes. It shows no recognizable similarity to dTDP-glucose 4,6-dehydratases, so it is unlikely to have this activity.

The sequence is a TGDS-like SDR-family dTDP-glucose 4,6-dehydratase (RmlB-type), with the TGxxGFIG NAD-binding and YxxxK catalytic motifs. Such enzymes are characterized as dTDP-glucose 4,6-dehydratases rather than UDP-glucose 4,6-dehydratases, though the sequence alone cannot fully rule out activity on UDP-glucose.

The sequence lacks the N-terminal Rossmann-fold GxxGxxG NAD(P)-binding motif and the catalytic YxxxK signature typical of SDR-family UDP-glucose 4,6-dehydratases. It shows no recognizable similarity to nucleotide-sugar dehydratases.

The sequence looks like a cytosolic dTDP-D-glucose 4,6-dehydratase (TGDS-like), an NAD-binding SDR sugar-nucleotide epimerase/dehydratase. Nothing in the sequence suggests targeting to the photoreceptor inner segment, though this is inferred from family resemblance rather than direct evidence.

The sequence has no recognizable motifs of photoreceptor-specific proteins such as opsins, phototransduction enzymes or ciliary/inner-segment trafficking factors. Its multiple N-glycosylation sites suggest a secreted or extracellular protein unrelated to the photoreceptor inner segment, though I could not identify the protein itself.

The sequence carries the NAD-binding Rossmann motif (GxxGFIG) and catalytic YxxxK motif typical of a nucleotide-sugar 4,6-dehydratase (TGDS-like, short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase family). That points to a cytosolic metabolic enzyme, with no receptor or signaling features.

The sequence has no recognizable features of proteins known to promote glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, such as GPCRs (GLP1R, FFAR1), ion channels, or glucose-sensing enzymes. It looks like a soluble protein of uncertain identity, possibly low-complexity or scrambled, and nothing in it supports this specific annotation.

The sequence is a class I fructose-bisphosphate aldolase A (an ALDOA ortholog nearly identical to human ALDOA). Its role is the glycolytic cleavage of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, and there is no established function in repairing or detoxifying damaged metabolites.

The sequence matches myeloperoxidase, a heme-containing peroxidase that makes hypochlorous acid; it is an enzyme, not a scaffold or adaptor. Nothing in the sequence points to protein-macromolecule adaptor activity.

The sequence has no recognizable adaptor or scaffolding domains (e.g., SH2/SH3, WD40, armadillo, PDZ) or other conserved motifs that would indicate it bridges macromolecules. The sequence has none of the hallmarks of a G protein-coupled receptor, G protein subunit, adenylate cyclase or known regulator of this pathway. In particular, it lacks the seven hydrophobic transmembrane segments, and nothing in it ties it to adenylate cyclase-activating GPCR signaling.

The sequence is LAMP2 (lysosome-associated membrane glycoprotein 2): a heavily N-glycosylated luminal domain, a single transmembrane helix, and the C-terminal lysosomal-targeting tail 'KHHHAGYEQF'. The sequence has no recognizable features of intraflagellar transport proteins, such as WD40/TPR repeats, dynein-2 motor domains or coiled-coil IFT-A scaffolds. Its many N-glycosylation motifs suggest a secreted or extracellular protein rather than a cytoplasmic ciliary transport component.

The sequence is a heavily N-glycosylated type I membrane protein with a proline-rich hinge and a C-terminal lysosomal-targeting motif (GLKHHHAGYEQF), which identifies it as LAMP1. That is a lysosomal membrane glycoprotein, not a multi-pass mitochondrial carrier that would transport coenzyme A.

The sequence has three repeated mitochondrial carrier (SLC25) domains with PX[DE]XX[KR] signature motifs and multiple transmembrane segments, consistent with a mitochondrial pyrimidine nucleotide carrier such as SLC25A33 or SLC25A36. The sequence has no recognizable domains of transcription-coupled repair factors such as CSB/ERCC6 helicase motifs, CSA WD40 repeats, UVSSA, XAB2 TPR repeats or Mfd. The sequence is a mitochondrial carrier (SLC25 family) solute transporter with no regulatory or EF-hand motifs. Nothing in the sequence points to a role in glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, although the specific carrier could not be confidently identified.

I could not match this sequence to any recognizable protein family, and it has none of the features of known regulators of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, such as GPCR, channel or secretory-machinery motifs. Given how rarely proteins carry this specific annotation, it most likely does not.

The sequence has no recognizable domains or motifs linked to TLR9 pathway regulators such as UNC93B1, CD14 or HMGB1, and its composition looks scrambled or atypical. Nothing in it supports annotating this protein with positive regulation of TLR9 signaling.

The sequence is spleen tyrosine kinase (SYK), with tandem SH2 domains followed by a C-terminal tyrosine kinase domain. Its known roles are in immunoreceptor signaling, and there is no evidence that it acts in transcription-coupled nucleotide-excision repair.

The sequence has no recognizable domains of transcription-coupled repair factors: no SNF2/helicase motifs like CSB, no WD40 repeats like CSA, and no UVSSA or XPA-like features. This sequence appears to be the human tyrosine kinase SYK, with tandem SH2 domains and a C-terminal kinase domain, which acts in immunoreceptor signaling. Nothing in the sequence suggests a role in non-stop mRNA decay, which relies on ribosome-rescue and SKI-complex factors, and I recall no such annotation for SYK.

The sequence does not show recognizable features of known non-stop decay factors, such as Pelota/Dom34, Hbs1/Ski7 GTPase motifs, Ski2 helicase motifs, or Ski3 TPR / Ski8 WD40 repeat architecture. The sequence has tandem N-terminal SH2 domains followed by a tyrosine kinase domain, which identifies it as a Syk-family kinase (ZAP-70-like) that signals downstream of immune receptors. Nothing in it suggests an enzyme that repairs damaged or toxic metabolites.

The sequence shows no recognizable motifs of known metabolite-repair enzymes, such as NAD(P)HX epimerase/dehydratase, L-2-hydroxyglutarate dehydrogenase, or the RidA or Nudix families. It appears to be a low-complexity or unusual protein with no evident catalytic domain for metabolite repair.

The sequence matches beta-arrestin-1 (ARRB1), an adaptor for GPCR desensitization and signaling. The sequence does not match any recognizable glucose-sensing, hexokinase, glucose-transporter or insulin-pathway family, and it lacks the motifs typical of proteins involved in intracellular glucose homeostasis. Because I could not identify the protein at all, this is a low-confidence call.

The sequence is beta-arrestin-1 (ARRB1), identified by its N-terminal arrestin-domain motif and C-terminal clathrin/AP2-binding region. The sequence appears to be a fragment with no clearly recognizable receptor, ligand or signaling-domain motifs, so it cannot be confidently tied to a cell surface receptor signaling pathway. The sequence is beta-arrestin 1 (ARRB1), which binds activated GPCRs, drives their desensitization and endocytosis, and acts as a signaling scaffold. The sequence does not match any known intraflagellar transport or dynein-2 component, and I see no WD40, TPR, dynein light-intermediate-chain or Tctex-like features. Nothing in it points to a role in retrograde ciliary transport.

The sequence matches beta-arrestin-1 (ARRB1). As I recall, beta-arrestins mediate Smoothened-dependent removal of GPCRs such as Gpr161 from the primary cilium, which counts as negatively regulating protein localization to the ciliary membrane.

The sequence has no recognizable domains or motifs linking it to ciliary membrane trafficking, such as tubby, ARF/ARL GTPase, BBSome or transition-zone features. Nothing in it supports a specific role in negatively regulating protein localization to the ciliary membrane.

The sequence is glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta (GSK3B), a Ser/Thr kinase acting in Wnt, insulin and microtubule signaling. Nothing known links it to transcription-coupled nucleotide-excision repair, a process carried out by proteins such as CSA, CSB and UVSSA.

The sequence is glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta (GSK3B), a cytoplasmic and nuclear Ser/Thr kinase acting in Wnt, insulin and microtubule regulation. It is not a dynein-2 or IFT-A complex component, and I know of no evidence for a direct role in intraciliary retrograde transport.
